steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a section for an encyclopedia article on adaptive grammars that surveys the adaptive formalisms in the literature, covering both the adaptive grammar formalisms and the adaptive machine formalisms, in historical order.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Two categories: adaptive grammars and adaptive machines
- Adaptive grammar formalisms, in order of first mention (Wegbreit, Christiansen, Burshteyn, Shutt, Boullier, Iwai, Jackson, Neto & Pistori, Carmi, Bravo)
- Adaptive machine formalisms (Shutt & Rubinstein, Neto)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive formalisms can be divided into two main categories. These are full grammar formalisms (adaptive grammars), and adaptive machines, which some grammar formalisms have been based on.

### Adaptive grammar formalisms

The following list of grammar formalisms is by no means complete. It lists formalisms that, by Shutt's definition above, are considered to be adaptive grammars (or have been classified by their own inventors as being adaptive grammars). They are listed in the historical order in which they were first mentioned in the literature.

### Extensible context-free grammars (Wegbreit)

Extensible context-free grammars were described in Wegbreit's doctoral dissertation in 1970. An extensible context-free grammar consists of a context-free grammar, and the rule set of this grammar is modified according to instructions that are output by a finite state transducer when it reads the terminal prefix during a leftmost derivation. So the rule set varies over the position in the generated string, but this variation ignores the hierarchical structure of the syntax tree. Shutt classified extensible context-free grammars as imperative.

### Christiansen grammars (Christiansen)

Christiansen grammars were first introduced in 1985 as Generative Grammars and were elaborated on more later. They are an adaptive extension of attribute grammars. The name Christiansen grammars was apparently given to them by Shutt, possibly because of a conflict with Chomsky generative grammars. Shutt classified Christiansen grammars as declarative.

The redoubling language L = \{ww | w \mbox{ is a letter}\} is demonstrated like this:

<program↓G> → <dcl↓G↑w> <body↓{w-rule}>

where w-rule =

<body↓G’> → w

<dcl↓G↑ch•w> → <char↓G↑ch> <dcl↓G↑w>

<dcl↓G↑<>> → <ε>

<char↓G↑a> → a

### Bottom-up modifiable grammars, top-down modifiable grammars, and USSA (Burshteyn)

Modifiable grammars were first introduced in May 1990 and later expanded on in December 1990. They explicitly provide a mechanism for adding and deleting rules during a parse. In response to the ACM SIGPLAN Notices responses, Burshteyn later modified his formalism, and in 1992 he introduced his adaptive Universal Syntax and Semantics Analyzer (USSA). Shutt classified these formalisms as imperative.

### Recursive adaptive grammars (Shutt)

Recursive Adaptive Grammars (RAGs) were introduced in 1993. They were an attempt to introduce a Turing powerful formalism that kept much of the elegance of context-free grammars. Shutt classifies RAGs himself as a declarative formalism.

### Dynamic grammars (Boullier)

- 1994; apparently first adaptive grammar family to rigorously put the time continuum of a parse in the notation
- sequence of grammars, each Gi differing over time; dynamic parser; type checking, extensible languages, polymorphism etc.

### Adaptive grammars (Iwai)

- 2000; Neto's adaptive automata applied to context-sensitive grammars; ? query, + addition, - deletion

### §-calculus (Jackson)

- 2000, most fully 2006; meta-ess; addition, deletion, modification of productions; syntactic predicates
- imperative and adaptive / time-space adaptive; others: analytic
- [example: redoubling language L = \{ww | w \in \{a,b\}^+\} + note on notation]

### Adaptive devices (Neto & Pistori)

- Neto 2001, Pistori 2003

### Adapser (Carmi)

- Adam Carmi 2002, LALR(1)-based, specifics not released

### Adaptive CFGs with appearance checking (Bravo)

- César Bravo 2004; appearance checking + adaptive CFGs (restricted Iwai); Turing powerful

### Adaptive machine formalisms

- not grammar formalisms; basis of grammar formalisms or adaptive in nature; historical order
- Self-modifying finite state automata (Shutt & Rubinstein): 1994, SMFAs, Turing powerful in restricted form
- Adaptive automata (Neto): 1994 structured pushdown automaton; core of adaptive automata theory (Iwai, Pistori, Bravo, others); inspection, addition, deletion

steps.text:
Adaptive formalisms can be divided into two main categories. These are full grammar formalisms (adaptive grammars), and adaptive machines, which some grammar formalisms have been based on.

### Adaptive grammar formalisms

The following list of grammar formalisms is by no means complete. It lists formalisms that, by Shutt's definition above, are considered to be adaptive grammars (or have been classified by their own inventors as being adaptive grammars). They are listed in the historical order in which they were first mentioned in the literature.

### Extensible context-free grammars (Wegbreit)

Extensible context-free grammars were described in Wegbreit's doctoral dissertation in 1970. An extensible context-free grammar consists of a context-free grammar, and the rule set of this grammar is modified according to instructions that are output by a finite state transducer when it reads the terminal prefix during a leftmost derivation. So the rule set varies over the position in the generated string, but this variation ignores the hierarchical structure of the syntax tree. Shutt classified extensible context-free grammars as imperative.

### Christiansen grammars (Christiansen)

Christiansen grammars were first introduced in 1985 as Generative Grammars and were elaborated on more later. They are an adaptive extension of attribute grammars. The name Christiansen grammars was apparently given to them by Shutt, possibly because of a conflict with Chomsky generative grammars. Shutt classified Christiansen grammars as declarative.

The redoubling language L = \{ww | w \mbox{ is a letter}\} is demonstrated like this:

<program↓G> → <dcl↓G↑w> <body↓{w-rule}>

where w-rule =

<body↓G’> → w

<dcl↓G↑ch•w> → <char↓G↑ch> <dcl↓G↑w>

<dcl↓G↑<>> → <ε>

<char↓G↑a> → a

### Bottom-up modifiable grammars, top-down modifiable grammars, and USSA (Burshteyn)

Modifiable grammars were first introduced in May 1990 and later expanded on in December 1990. They explicitly provide a mechanism for adding and deleting rules during a parse. In response to the ACM SIGPLAN Notices responses, Burshteyn later modified his formalism, and in 1992 he introduced his adaptive Universal Syntax and Semantics Analyzer (USSA). Shutt classified these formalisms as imperative.

### Recursive adaptive grammars (Shutt)

Recursive Adaptive Grammars (RAGs) were introduced in 1993. They were an attempt to introduce a Turing powerful formalism that kept much of the elegance of context-free grammars. Shutt classifies RAGs himself as a declarative formalism.

### Dynamic grammars (Boullier)

Boullier introduced his dynamic grammars in 1994. They appear to be the first adaptive grammar family of grammars to rigorously introduce the notion of a time continuum of a parse as part of the notation of the grammar formalism itself. Dynamic grammars are a sequence of grammars, and each grammar Gi differs in some way from the other grammars in the sequence, over time. Boullier's main paper on dynamic grammars also defines a dynamic parser, which is the machine that does a parse against these grammars. It also shows examples of how his formalism can handle things like type checking, extensible languages, polymorphism, and other constructs that are usually considered to be in the semantic domain of programming language translation.

### Adaptive grammars (Iwai)

In 2000 the work of Iwai took the adaptive automata of Neto further by applying adaptive automata to context-sensitive grammars. Iwai's adaptive grammars (note the qualifier by name) allow three operations during a parse: ? query (similar in some ways to a syntactic predicate, but tied to inspecting rules from which modifications are chosen), + addition, and - deletion (it shares the last two with its predecessor adaptive automata).

### §-calculus (Jackson)

The §-Calculus (§ here is pronounced meta-ess) was introduced in 2000 and most fully discussed in 2006. It allows for the explicit addition, deletion, and modification of productions within a grammar, and it also provides syntactic predicates. Its creator self-classifies this formalism as both imperative and adaptive, or, more specifically, as a time-space adaptive grammar formalism, and others further classified it as an analytic formalism.

The redoubling language L = \{ww | w \in \{a,b\}^+\} is demonstrated like this:

grammar ww {

S ::= #phi(A.X<-"") R;

R ::= $C('[ab]') #phi(A.X<-A.X C) #phi(N<=A.X) N | R;

(Note on notation: In the above example, the statements identify the points in the production R that modify the grammar explicitly. represents a global modification (over time) and the statement identifies a local modification (over space). The statement in the S production effectively declares a global production called A.X by placing the empty string into that production before its reference by R.)

### Adaptive devices (Neto & Pistori)

Adaptive devices were first described by Neto in 2001, and Pistori later enhanced and expanded on them in 2003.

### Adapser (Carmi)

Adam Carmi introduced an LALR(1)-based adaptive grammar formalism called Adapser in 2002. The specifics of the formalism do not seem to have been released.

### Adaptive CFGs with appearance checking (Bravo)

In 2004, César Bravo introduced the idea of merging the concept of appearance checking with adaptive context-free grammars, which are a restricted form of Iwai's adaptive grammars. He showed that these new grammars, called Adaptive CFGs with Appearance Checking, are Turing powerful.

### Adaptive machine formalisms

The formalisms in the list below are not grammar formalisms, but they either serve as the basis of full grammar formalisms, or they are included here because they are adaptive in nature. They are listed in the historical order in which they were first mentioned in the literature.

Self-modifying finite state automata (Shutt & Rubinstein)

Self-Modifying Finite State Automata (SMFAs) were introduced in 1994 by Shutt and Rubinstein, and they are shown to be Turing powerful in a restricted form.

Adaptive automata (Neto)

In 1994, Neto introduced a machine that he called a structured pushdown automaton. This is the core of adaptive automata theory as it was pursued by Iwai, Pistori, Bravo and others. The formalism allows for the operations of inspection (similar to syntactic predicates, as noted above for Iwai's adaptive grammars), addition, and deletion of rules.

Adaptive formalisms may be divided into two main categories: full grammar formalisms (adaptive grammars), and adaptive machines, on which some grammar formalisms have been based.

### Adaptive grammar formalisms

The following is a list (by no means complete) of grammar formalisms that, by Shutt's definition above, are considered to be (or have been classified by their own inventors as being) adaptive grammars. They are listed in historical order of first mention in the literature.

### Extensible context-free grammars (Wegbreit)

Described in Wegbreit's doctoral dissertation in 1970,[1] an extensible context-free grammar consists of a context-free grammar whose rule set is modified according to instructions output by a finite state transducer when reading the terminal prefix during a leftmost derivation. The rule set therefore varies over position in the generated string, but this variation ignores the hierarchical structure of the syntax tree. Extensible context-free grammars were classified by Shutt as imperative.[2]

### Christiansen grammars (Christiansen)

First introduced in 1985 as Generative Grammars[3] and later elaborated upon,[4] Christiansen grammars (apparently so named by Shutt, possibly due to a conflict with Chomsky generative grammars) are an adaptive extension of attribute grammars. Christiansen grammars were classified by Shutt as declarative.[2]

The redoubling language L = \{ww | w \mbox{ is a letter}\} is demonstrated as follows:[4]

<program↓G> → <dcl↓G↑w> <body↓{w-rule}>

where w-rule =

<body↓G’> → w

<dcl↓G↑ch•w> → <char↓G↑ch> <dcl↓G↑w>

<dcl↓G↑<>> → <ε>

<char↓G↑a> → a

### Bottom-up modifiable grammars, top-down modifiable grammars, and USSA (Burshteyn)

First introduced in May 1990[5] and later expanded upon in December 1990,[6] modifiable grammars explicitly provide a mechanism for adding and deleting rules during a parse. In response to the ACM SIGPLAN Notices responses, Burshteyn later modified his formalism and introduced his adaptive Universal Syntax and Semantics Analyzer (USSA) in 1992.[7] These formalisms were classified by Shutt as imperative.[2]

### Recursive adaptive grammars (Shutt)

Introduced in 1993, Recursive Adaptive Grammars (RAGs) were an attempt to introduce a Turing powerful formalism that kept much of the elegance of context-free grammars.[2] Shutt self-classifies RAGs as a declarative formalism.

### Dynamic grammars (Boullier)

Boullier's dynamic grammars, introduced in 1994,[8] appear to be the first adaptive grammar family of grammars to rigorously introduce the notion of a time continuum of a parse as part of the notation of the grammar formalism itself.[9] Dynamic grammars are a sequence of grammars, with each grammar Gi differing in some way from the other grammars in the sequence, over time. Boullier's main paper on dynamic grammars also defines a dynamic parser, the machine that carries out a parse against these grammars, and shows examples of how his formalism can handle such things as type checking, extensible languages, polymorphism, and other constructs typically considered to be in the semantic domain of programming language translation.

### Adaptive grammars (Iwai)

The work of Iwai in 2000[10] takes the adaptive automata of Neto[11] further by applying adaptive automata to context-sensitive grammars. Iwai's adaptive grammars (note the qualifier by name) allow three operations during a parse: ? query (similar in some respects to a syntactic predicate, but tied to inspection of rules from which modifications are chosen), + addition, and - deletion (which it shares with its predecessor adaptive automata).

### §-calculus (Jackson)

Introduced in 2000[12] and most fully discussed in 2006,[9] the §-Calculus (§ here pronounced meta-ess) allows for the explicit addition, deletion, and modification of productions within a grammar, and also provides for syntactic predicates. This formalism is self-classified by its creator as both imperative and adaptive, or, more specifically, as a time-space adaptive grammar formalism, and has been further classified by others as an analytic formalism.[13,14]

The redoubling language L = \{ww | w \in \{a,b\}^+\} is demonstrated as follows:

grammar ww {

S ::= #phi(A.X<-"") R;

R ::= $C('[ab]') #phi(A.X<-A.X C) #phi(N<=A.X) N | R;

(Note on notation: In the above example, the statements identify the points in the production R that modify the grammar explicitly. represents a global modification (over time) and the statement identifies a local modification (over space). The statement in the S production effectively declares a global production called A.X by placing the empty string into that production before its reference by R.)

### Adaptive devices (Neto & Pistori)

First described by Neto in 2001,[15] adaptive devices were later enhanced and expanded upon by Pistori in 2003.[16]

### Adapser (Carmi)

In 2002,[17] Adam Carmi introduced an LALR(1)-based adaptive grammar formalism known as Adapser. Specifics of the formalism do not appear to have been released.

### Adaptive CFGs with appearance checking (Bravo)

In 2004,[13] César Bravo introduced the idea of merging the concept of appearance checking[18] with adaptive context-free grammars, a restricted form of Iwai's adaptive grammars,[10] and showed these new grammars, called Adaptive CFGs with Appearance Checking, to be Turing powerful.

### Adaptive machine formalisms

The formalisms listed below, while not grammar formalisms, either serve as the basis of full grammar formalisms or are included here because they are adaptive in nature. They are listed in historical order of first mention in the literature.

Self-modifying finite state automata (Shutt & Rubinstein)

Introduced in 1994 by Shutt and Rubinstein,[19] Self-Modifying Finite State Automata (SMFAs) are shown to be Turing powerful in a restricted form.

Adaptive automata (Neto)

In 1994,[11] Neto introduced the machine he called a structured pushdown automaton, the core of adaptive automata theory as pursued by Iwai,[10] Pistori,[16] Bravo[13] and others. This formalism allows for the operations of inspection (similar to syntactic predicates, as noted above for Iwai's adaptive grammars), addition, and deletion of rules.
